Thank you. Thank you to Chair Andrews. Good afternoon to the Board of Supervisors and the School Board. Thank you for the introduction. I just also want to thank Ms. Koumizawa for all of her partnership, and really just so many people in the back. I know we're listening online to really put together this presentation, try and take really complex topics, make them simple, have creative strategy thinking, and all of the things that go to that year round.

I really appreciate whether we're talking about the capital budget or the county's health fund, just the partnership that we have between mine that goes through all the thinking year round. So just to begin to frame today, as we dive into what is scheduled to be a three-hour work session, I'd often like to start with the board of supervisors, framing everything in the context of the board's strategic plan.

This is the plan that was adopted three years ago this fall, and it includes six goals, one of which is education and learning. Now, education and learning is one of six, and it's also, as the board discusses, it is the largest component of the county's operating budget.

It is also the largest component of the county's debt service and capital budgets. So this is a topic when the school board had their strategic plan, and I'm sure that will be part of their comments later. But you're really to ground this as the Board of Supervisors through October and November has spent a lot of time discussing where are we in different areas, whether it's public safety in Goal 1 or the economic development that's part of Goal 4.

But today is really going to be focused on Goal 5. And when I think about the capital budget, and this is really a forward-looking conversation today, and I think of the partnership and all of the good work and thought that comes from these teams, I thought, how do I try and encapsulate at least just one slide in a rear view of where we've been?

So perhaps it's because I'm analytically minded, but I said I can make a chart to show that. So if you all can bear with me, this will be the most complicated chart that I showed today. So what I have here, oh, and I'm sorry, the animations didn't come in in this version. So bear with me.

Now, it's tough to describe all of the changes that have happened in summary. I have some that I'll walk through, but to have such a change going from debt service payments of roughly $12 million to $13 million and roughly $6 million, evolving to the out years of debt service payments of just under $30 million and just under $20 million, I think it's a lot of intentionality, a lot of partnership, a lot of long-range multiple years plan.

When you get an outward slope in the mountain, that reflects years the county did not issue bonds, but debt has been retired for expenses in the last 20 years. So that's why we have a little bit of those, you know, kind of the mountain range outline. After that happened, the board of supervisors, they issued bonds to implement those projects. The debt service was paid, and the board of supervisors raised the tax rate to support the debt service for that increased cost. Moving ahead, we go into fiscal year '22.

County's body issuance, and this included improvements at Crozet, Red Hill, and Scottsville, among the highlights. I'm really just trying to highlight on those more notable items that we think of as the generational investments that we own with its current facilities.

Moving ahead to fiscal year 26, we see really the portions of the Southern Elementary School, or the Mountain View Upper Elementary School, the Ace Academy, or High School Center 2, and the renovation projects really begin to ramp up. So long-range financial planning is a regular process the Board of Supervisors inducts to really think through are the decisions made today If not, what are the strategies in the long term that can begin to shape that trajectory very differently?

It's not only about just dollars. There could be policy levers. There could be other strategies that you can pursue. We'll have the best projection we have, and the exercise of planning will be more important than the plan itself because we'll continue to adapt to new information, strategies, and how that plays out.

This includes me and the county's obligations and also initiatives that would move forward the board strategic plan.

So there are two major changes driving that, first of which is the board of supervisors increase the real estate tax rate in this calendar year. The school board will also have obligations as we open two schools next year and other operating pressures as well. So there will be certainly challenges in the next couple of years to work from, but by that long-term planning and multi-year approach, there is opportunity that can be met on the horizon. So to kind of understand a little more about that opportunity, what are the strategies to really shape that outcome a little bit differently in the county's revenue picture?

I want to focus on something that the board has been, board supervisors have been very focused on this year. What is the makeup of the county's tax base? And so this is a chart that shows by category. These are the state code categories and how properties are assessed. We can see that from 2015 to 2025, the county's residential tax base increased from 61% to 68%.

That growth came at the tradeoff for declines in the commercial and industrial sector as well as agricultural. And you all can see the declines there. So why this matters so much, because a dollar of revenue is a dollar of revenue wherever it comes from, but it's really about the expenditure side.

Because while all of these different categories can generate revenue, they're very different at what it costs to provide services in these categories. So earlier this year, the board received a report for the cost of community services study. And so it's a different breakdown in the analysis, though the words are the same in terms of residential, commercial, industrial, and agricultural.

So the general point remains the same. I think we know this intrinsically, that when it comes to residential development, it costs more to serve those residents than it does for the revenue they collect from those. The opposite is true with commercial and industrial. For every dollar of revenue collected, it costs on average $0.30 to provide those services.

So as we've seen over 10 years, as that has shifted from 61% to 68%, commercial declining from 15% to 11%, that really begins to shift some of the burden onto the residential tax base. And so one of the reasons we know residential is the highest is that is where the school population comes from.

That is the largest part of the county budget, and that is where students come from. So this does not mean when it comes to rebalancing the county's tax base as a way to generate revenues. It's not done to chase commercial and industrial. In that regard, there is a plan for that.

And earlier this year, as I feel like I'm giving highlights of the board's work in the last year, The board adopted an updated economic development strategic plan. So there's a lot of focus when it comes to commercial, industrial, and even agricultural. What does that look like? Across the top, there are three industries that are targeted, intelligence and national security, biolife sciences, and agribusiness.

Now, it's not just about attracting business as well. There are strategies in empowering talent and competing for investment. There's a lot of alignment when it comes to empowering talent, because you may hear phrases such as workforce readiness, workforce development. Another good synonym for that is education. How do we have our future generations ready for this evolving world that we're going into?

And so I'll back up. When we talk about that out-year picture of the revenues increasing, the governor has been here twice this fall for the announcement of AstraZeneca located in the northern part of the county. The continued development of Afton Scientific is a more homegrown business. And really the opportunities that will come with that, and even smaller examples, it's not a one-size-fits-all.

We have the Home Depot re-development as the value of Fashion Square declined over time. Now there's an anchor tenant there, and we'll see in the future how does that begin to develop. How does all of these other strategies begin to come together to change that tax base and provide something different? What was once a plan a few years ago is now seeing more tangible results of that, and that will continue in the future as this is built out.

So with that said in the revenues, there is some uncertainty we have to navigate in the short term because all of these changes are not going to happen overnight. So the county consults with a group from Virginia Tech to do an annual economic outlook report. The big takeaways we had there is, first, in the national economy, the economy is slowing down compared to prior years.

We are still seeing modest growth. The economy has been very resilient nationally, but we also have this very big continued uncertainty with federal policy shifts that are occurring. Second is that Virginia's economy is cooling faster than the nation's economy, at least through the first half of fiscal year 25.

It's caught staff's attention because historically Virginia will outperform the nation at economic performance. But because Virginia is so heavily leveraged in the federal government and as that federal landscape changes, and about 42% of Virginia's economy is based out on Northern Virginia.

So as that is impacted, that has a disproportionate impact to the overall state. So right now in the county's revenues, we don't see any impact of this directly, but what might that mean to future state budgets? What might that mean to how that may indirectly impact localities? We'll see as that plays out, we'll continue to watch this closely, because right now, based on our current year performance, Alton Morrow County has got a strong economic base to work through.

And because of that, because of the board's approach and discipline to your planning, thinking ahead, and the strategy, that provides us a really good scope to head on to this uncertainty for the next few years. So again, in summary, we're in a very different trend from what it were this time last year, prior years, for the five-year plan summary in the past.

We do have two very distinct periods in those five years. With an evolving revenue outlook, revenues we would project to continue to grow, but it would not be at the rate that we have seen in the last few years. And also that shifting landscape can impact expenditures as well. And then in the longer term, the strategies continuing to play out to change that tax base will provide an ability to continue to meet obligations and more robustly advance strategic plan goals.

So with that, I'm going to shift gears, and I'm going to provide an overview of what is currently in the appropriated capital budget and the adopted CIP. What we hear from today from the schools, and I'll touch on this briefly for county government, is where is the request in those things ahead?

But just to get us grounded, there are some projects we're not talking about because they're under construction or will be soon. So just taking a moment, because terminology is important, when you talk about the capital improvements plan. We are referring to capital budget. That is the appropriated budget. Legal authority is there.

Things are under contract. Dirt is moving. Those are things that are in the capital budget. When we talk about the CIP, it's really referring to years two through five of the plan, where those projects are adopted, planning is underway to implement those when it becomes legally appropriate.

Just as I talked about earlier in multi-year planning, we also have to plan for the multi-year impacts.

What does it cost to run the day-to-day impact when those good projects are constructed and then put into service? Where does the annual debt service? Capital projects are generational investments, and so when it takes 20 years for that debt commitment, that is an ongoing commitment we always have to be preparing for, as well as ensuring that we're operationally ready to implement those projects.

So at a very high level, we have the CIP revenues for the five years total over $300 million. The two big revenues that fund the majority of the CIP are cash equity. That comes from formula allocations by the board of supervisors.

Also, any one-time money that either the board or the school board that may come available that can be applied into the capital budget. The second category is planned borrower proceeds, which is the majority of this. We're, again, generational investments, generational paybacks with 20-year debt service.

And so the county will strategize for those projects that are eligible to be borrowed for. So these are two charts that if the public listening has followed the capital discussion before, they may look familiar. That red line is the policy cap that the board of supervisors have set, and that's informed by national standards of what a triple-triple-A bond agency would look like.

So currently, based on what's approved with the major projects like the courts, Preventa Futures, the three schools, everything else in the CIP. The tightest area, for anyone who may be eagle-eyed, is actually on the area on the left, where there's about $72 million of capacity if we were to go to 9% on that policy.

I'm going to come back to that at the end of the presentation and talk a little bit more about that figure and strategies for the future. Charts about debt are one thing, but it really gets back to the question of why do we have a triple-triple-A bond rating in the first place? This is a common question that I make it.

I'll share that when I'm discussing with folks in the community or just others, when I talk about municipal bonds, sometimes I can lose someone's attention. So I'm going to frame this with apologies to our CFO and my supervisor. But this is one where I want to put this in the realm of what does it mean if you're an individual with an triple-triple-A bond rating?

So out moral, they had two ratings that were retained in 2003. The third was attained in 2013. There are only 54 of the 3,000-plus counties as of last month in the entire United States who had this. Of those 54, 13 are in Virginia. So when we look at a lot of our peers and benchmarking, they are just like us in their financial management.

So there are a lot of benefits to a moderated agency. And so we think about this. If you're an individual, you have a perfect credit rating if you're in this situation. And so what does this mean? One element, and I think we can all understand this, is that future flexibility. If you think of an individual, you think of the first thing they would need to do is pay your mortgage or pay your rent every month.

The lower that amount is relative to your overall income, the more flexibility you have to do everything else, whether it be for your quality of life, your basic needs, whatever that may look like. And so again, that future flexibility for localities where they may not have this rating and they have much higher debt load, they don't have as much flexibility to do something different on a year-to-year basis.

Because again, debt is an important tool. Bonds are an important tool to move forward capital projects, but it is a 20-year commitment. Second is when you have such a high credit rate agency, if you're this individual, you get the best possible rates in the market. And so you can imagine a situation if you were an individual and you needed to do a home renovation project or maybe a major car repair.

What would happen if you needed to do that and immediately you had nine mechanics or nine contractors show up at your door to give you what that would look like? You're probably going to be in a pretty great situation, and that is exactly what happens when the county issues bonds. In 2023, there were nine major financial institutions who were ready to purchase those bonds, and that allows the county to get the lowest possible interest rate as those bonds are paid back over 20 years.

Finally, in the case of an emergency, if there was every major natural disaster or sudden shock where the county did need to borrow unexpectedly or short-term, the county would be able to access that cash and be able to do so at the best possible rate relative to the market. So that's just a little bit more of kind of some real-world examples on how that AAA plays out, whether you are a municipality or whether you are an individual with a very high credit rating.

On behalf of the school board, Dr. Haas, and the ACPS staff, we welcome this opportunity to discuss how we can best partner to build for the future of our students and the community. We have provided you with the detailed capital priorities and background information for all of the projects listed, and I hope you've had the opportunity to look at it.

The discussion of school capital investment is a discussion about building for the county's future. Schools are central to every community. They provide a sense of place where students and families connect and engage in shared life experiences. Schools also reflect the quality and image of the communities that they serve and are critical drivers of economic development.

Any family or business considering locating to a community and the quality of schools regularly ranks at or near the top of their list of priorities. We are proud of the learning opportunities we create for our students and the notable progress we've made to ensure that all students have the chance to learn, dream, and grow into the future they imagine for themselves.

We especially want to thank you, the county, for prioritizing the funding for our new Mountain View Upper Elementary School and the Albemarle Career Exploration Center at LLC, both of which will open next fall and be wonderful learning environments for our students.

We've also begun planning for the opening of North Point Elementary School in the 29-30 school year. these two elementary schools plus the 35,000 square foot addition to Crozet Elementary School that opened three years ago will make a significant dent toward expanding our elementary school capacity. But we are still playing catch up on our capital construction needs. There is no doubt that investment in school capital projects is essential for building a future for our students and our community.

As the Yale School of Economics notes, capital investment in schools improves test scores and raises housing values. And so together, we have an obligation to our constituents to provide school facilities that reflect the quality of life families and businesses expect in Alabama County.
